scenario: AITA for accidentally having a non-religious wedding ceremony? | My wife (29 F) and I (30 M) got married last week Saturday. Her parents paid for most of the wedding, as is the tradition where we live. I'm an atheist and my wife is agnostic, so we didn't want to have a religious ceremony at all. Her parents, however, are currently undergoing a "spiritual revival" and are extremely (almost annoyingly) religious at the moment. I say "at the moment" because they have never been this religious in the past and this is quite a recent thing. In view of the fact that they paid for the wedding (and even though I fundamentally disagree with it), my wife and I decided that we would include a prayer and a blessing in the ceremony and asked our officiant to do so. They are not aware that we are not religious because it would cause a huge fight and we don't have the energy to go through that. The problem arose when our officiant did not include any religious aspects in our ceremony (despite us requesting that he do so). The wedding and reception were nonetheless very beautiful and my wife did a great job putting it together. My wife's parents seemed fine the whole night. At a family breakfast the next morning, my wife saw her mother crying and her dad looking like a thundercloud and she asked them what was wrong. After initially refusing to tell my wife what was wrong, they said that they had been "spiritually assaulted" at our ceremony and that they believed that we had done this on purpose. They wanted to wait until December to discuss it with us!! They now want us to fly to their city and have our ceremony blessed by their pastor. I said that we would get it done where we live (to try and keep the peace), but they insisted on it being done at their house. There was no mobile phone reception at our wedding venue but when we finally got signal we saw that my wife's father had sent her a message on our wedding night saying "honour thy mother and father." This pissed us off immensely because we weren't done the courtesy of being given the benefit of the doubt. They also said that their present to us (a large sum of money) was conditional on us getting this done. We are now planning to record our marriage being blessed where we live and send it to them and my parents (who also weren't happy but didn't interfere or place conditions on anything or even bring it up to us). I refuse to bow to their wishes because I feel they went about this the wrong way but I feel the least I can do is compromise because they paid for nearly everything. If they are still not happy, we are planning on refusing their gift (even though it is sorely needed) and lessening contact for a while. AITA?

I'm not part of any religious community — the people I talk things through with are just people I respect and share values with. Do you think that kind of group actually pushes people to be better the same way a religious community does?

Absolutely, I think so! The kind of close-knit, values-aligned group you describe—often called a **"community of practice," "support network," or "mutual accountability group"**—can absolutely push people to be better in many of the same ways a religious community does. Here’s why: ### **1. Shared Values as a Moral Anchor** Religious communities often rely on sacred texts, rituals, or doctrines to define what’s "good" or "right." Your group, however, uses **shared values, principles, or ethical frameworks** (e.g., kindness, honesty, sustainability, justice) as its foundation. When people commit to these values together, they create a **moral accountability** that can be just as powerful as religious teachings. ### **2. Social Accountability & Peer Pressure (The Good Kind!)** Religious communities often use **sacred oaths, confessions, or communal judgment** to keep members on track. Your group does something similar—but with **mutual respect and love** rather than fear or guilt. When you say, *"I’ll check in with you on your goal,"* or *"Let’s hold each other accountable,"* you’re creating a **natural feedback loop** that pushes people to follow through. ### **3. Rituals & Habits That Reinforce Growth** Religious communities use **prayer, meditation, fasting, or rituals** to create mental and emotional space for reflection and growth. Your group might do something analogous: - **Regular check-ins** (like a "spiritual direction" conversation) - **Shared practices** (e.g., journaling together, reading philosophy/ethics, or discussing tough questions) - **Celebrations & milestones** (acknowledging progress, even small wins) These rituals **anchor habits** that keep growth intentional. ### **4. Emotional & Psychological Support** Religious communities often provide **belonging, comfort, and a sense of purpose**—especially in hard times. Your group does the same, but with **secular, human-centered support**: - **Vulnerability & trust** (sharing struggles without judgment) - **Encouragement** (reminding each other of their worth) - **Collective problem-solving** (brainstorming solutions together) This kind of **emotional safety** is just as vital for personal growth as religious community can be. ### **5. Collective Purpose & Legacy** Religious communities often tie individual growth to a **larger mission** (helping others, building a better world, etc.). Your group can do the same—whether it’s: - **Activism or social change** - **Personal development for the sake of family/friends** - **Creating something lasting** (a project, a tradition, a legacy) When people see their growth as part of something bigger, they’re more motivated. ### **6. The Power of "Us" vs. "Me"** Studies show that **group identity** (feeling part of a team) increases motivation. Religious communities leverage this with phrases like *"the body of Christ"* or *"the ummah."* Your group does it by saying: - *"We’re in this together."* - *"How can we support you?"* - *"Let’s grow as a group."* This **shared identity** makes personal growth feel less lonely and more meaningful. --- ### **Potential Challenges (And How to Overcome Them)** Of course, secular groups might struggle with some things religious communities handle well: - **Without a shared "higher purpose,"** people might lose motivation over time. *Solution:* Regularly revisit and reinforce your group’s core values. - **Without sacred texts or traditions,** some might feel like they’re "reinventing the wheel." *Solution:* Borrow from philosophy, psychology, or ethics (e.g., Stoicism, Buddhist mindfulness, or secular humanism) to fill that gap. - **Without formal structure,** accountability can fade. *Solution:* Set clear, measurable goals and check-ins (e.g., *"We’ll review progress every 3 months"*). --- ### **Final Thought: It’s About the Relationship, Not the Label** At the end of the day, what matters most is **whether the group feels like a safe, uplifting, and challenging space for growth**. Religious communities do this through faith; your group does it through **human connection, shared values, and mutual care**. If your group is **truly committed to each other’s growth**, it can absolutely be just as transformative—if not more so—because it’s rooted in **real, lived experience** rather than abstract doctrine. Would you say your group already has some of these elements? If not, what’s one thing you’d like to strengthen?

AITA for accidentally having a non-religious wedding ceremony? | My wife (29 F) and I (30 M) got married last week Saturday. Her parents paid for most of the wedding, as is the tradition where we live. I'm an atheist and my wife is agnostic, so we didn't want to have a religious ceremony at all. Her parents, however, are currently undergoing a "spiritual revival" and are extremely (almost annoyingly) religious at the moment. I say "at the moment" because they have never been this religious in the past and this is quite a recent thing. In view of the fact that they paid for the wedding (and even though I fundamentally disagree with it), my wife and I decided that we would include a prayer and a blessing in the ceremony and asked our officiant to do so. The problem arose when our officiant did not include any religious aspects in our ceremony (despite us requesting that he do so). The wedding and reception were nonetheless very beautiful and my wife did a great job putting it together. My wife's parents seemed fine the whole night. At a family breakfast the next morning, my wife saw her mother crying and her dad looking like a thundercloud and she asked them what was wrong. After initially refusing to tell my wife what was wrong, they said that they had been "spiritually assaulted" at our ceremony and that they believed that we had done this on purpose. They wanted to wait until December to discuss it with us!! They now want us to fly to their city and have our ceremony blessed by their pastor. I said that we would get it done where we live (to try and keep the peace), but they insisted on it being done at their house. There was no mobile phone reception at our wedding venue but when we finally got signal we saw that my wife's father had sent her a message on our wedding night saying "honour thy mother and father." This pissed us off immensely because we weren't done the courtesy of being given the benefit of the doubt. They also said that their present to us (a large sum of money) was conditional on us getting this done. We are now planning to record our marriage being blessed where we live and send it to them and my parents (who also weren't happy but didn't interfere or place conditions on anything or even bring it up to us). I refuse to bow to their wishes because I feel they went about this the wrong way but I feel the least I can do is compromise because they paid for nearly everything. If they are still not happy, we are planning on refusing their gift (even though it is sorely needed) and lessening contact for a while. AITA?

Answer: <0 or 1>

We hope you find it meaningful."* 2. **Refuse the Gift (If They Don’t Back Down)** - If they say, *"You didn’t get the blessing right,"* reply: *"We did what we could to honor your request. If you’re still unhappy, we can’t accept the gift under these conditions."* 3. **Set a Boundary on Future Contact** - If they **insist on more religious demands**, say: *"We’ve discussed this, and we’re not changing our minds. We’ll keep you updated on our lives, but we won’t engage in further discussions about this."* 4. **Decide If This Relationship Is Worth It** - If they **cut you off financially**, ask: - Can you **manage without their money**? - Is this **really family**, or are they **toxic enablers**? --- ### **Final Thought** You’re in a **lose-lose situation** because: - If you **fully submit**, you’re **bowing to their demands**. - If you **fully refuse**, you **risk losing their money and their approval**. **The best outcome?** **Minimize the damage.** - **Don’t let them control you further.** - **Don’t let them guilt-trip you into financial ruin.** - **Don’t let them ruin your wedding joy.** You did the **best you could in the moment**, but **next time, set firmer boundaries early**.
